mathprize-olympiad-2010-01.title: Bound each element
mathprize-olympiad-2010-01.body:
Write $S=\{a_1<a_2<\dots<a_{100}\}$. We claim $a_k\le 2k-1$ for every $k$.

Suppose instead $a_k\ge 2k$ for some $k$. For $j=1,\dots,k$ the numbers $j$ and $a_k-j$ are positive integers (as $a_k-j\ge k>0$) with sum $a_k\in S$. By hypothesis, for each $j$ at least one of $j$, $a_k-j$ lies in $S$, and both are smaller than $a_k$.

Since $j\le k\le a_k-k$, the numbers $1,\dots,k$ and $a_k-k,\dots,a_k-1$ can overlap only in the value $k=a_k-k$ (when $a_k=2k$), and in that case the pair for $j=k$ is just $\{k\}$. So the $k$ pairs are pairwise disjoint (as sets), and choosing one element of $S$ from each pair gives $k$ distinct elements of $S$ smaller than $a_k$.

But only $k-1$ elements of $S$ are smaller than $a_k$ (namely $a_1,\dots,a_{k-1}$), a contradiction. Hence $a_k\le 2k-1$.

Summing,
$$\sum_{k=1}^{100}a_k\le\sum_{k=1}^{100}(2k-1)=100^2=10{,}000.\ ∎$$

mathprize-olympiad-2010-02.title: Split into odd part and power of 2
mathprize-olympiad-2010-02.body:
**Case 1: $n$ odd.** Then $2$ is invertible mod $n$; pick $a$ with $2a\equiv1\pmod n$ and $b=0$. Then $4a^2+9b^2-1=(2a-1)(2a+1)$ is divisible by $n$.

**Case 2: $3\nmid n$.** Then $3$ is invertible mod $n$; pick $b$ with $3b\equiv1\pmod n$ and $a=0$. Then $4a^2+9b^2-1=(3b-1)(3b+1)$ is divisible by $n$.

**General case.** Write $n=n_1n_2$ where $n_2$ is the largest power of $2$ dividing $n$ and $n_1$ is odd, so $\gcd(n_1,n_2)=1$. A power of $2$ is not divisible by $3$, so Case 2 gives $a_2,b_2$ with $n_2\mid 4a_2^2+9b_2^2-1$; Case 1 gives $a_1,b_1$ with $n_1\mid 4a_1^2+9b_1^2-1$.

By the Chinese Remainder Theorem choose integers $a\equiv a_1\pmod{n_1}$, $a\equiv a_2\pmod{n_2}$ and $b\equiv b_1\pmod{n_1}$, $b\equiv b_2\pmod{n_2}$. Modulo $n_1$ we get $4a^2+9b^2-1\equiv4a_1^2+9b_1^2-1\equiv0$, and modulo $n_2$ similarly $\equiv0$. Since $n_1,n_2$ are coprime, $n=n_1n_2$ divides $4a^2+9b^2-1$. ∎

mathprize-olympiad-2010-03.title: Two cases on the size of $p$
mathprize-olympiad-2010-03.body:
Note $24-9\sqrt7>0$ (since $9\sqrt7=\sqrt{567}<\sqrt{576}=24$). It suffices to show $|p-q\sqrt7|\ge\dfrac{24-9\sqrt7}{|q|}$.

**Case 1: $|p|\le\frac83|q|$.** Since $\sqrt7$ is irrational and $q\ne0$, $p^2-7q^2$ is a nonzero integer, so $|p-q\sqrt7|\cdot|p+q\sqrt7|\ge1$. Hence
$$|p-q\sqrt7|\ge\frac1{|p|+|q|\sqrt7}\ge\frac{1}{\left(\frac83+\sqrt7\right)|q|}=\frac{3}{(8+3\sqrt7)|q|}=\frac{3(8-3\sqrt7)}{|q|}=\frac{24-9\sqrt7}{|q|},$$
using $(8+3\sqrt7)(8-3\sqrt7)=64-63=1$.

**Case 2: $|p|>\frac83|q|$.** Then $\left|\frac pq\right|>\frac83$.

- If $|q|\ge3$: $\left|\frac pq-\sqrt7\right|\ge\left|\frac pq\right|-\sqrt7>\frac83-\sqrt7=\frac{24-9\sqrt7}{9}\ge\frac{24-9\sqrt7}{q^2}$, because $q^2\ge9$.
- If $|q|\in\{1,2\}$: $|p|>\frac83|q|$ forces $|p|\ge3|q|$ (for $|q|=1$, $|p|\ge3$; for $|q|=2$, $|p|>\frac{16}3$ so $|p|\ge6$). Then $\left|\frac pq\right|\ge3$ and $\left|\frac pq-\sqrt7\right|\ge3-\sqrt7>0.35$, while $24-9\sqrt7<24-9\cdot2.64=0.24$. So the left side exceeds $24-9\sqrt7\ge\frac{24-9\sqrt7}{q^2}$.

In every case the inequality holds. ∎

mathprize-olympiad-2010-04.title: Strong induction on $n$
mathprize-olympiad-2010-04.body:
We prove the claim by strong induction on $n$; the case $n=0$ is trivial. Let $n\ge1$ and assume the claim for all smaller sizes.

Let $L$ be a largest subset of $S$ consisting of all points of $S$ on one vertical line or on one horizontal line; by symmetry say the vertical line. Let $k=|L|\ge1$.

**Aligned pairs between $L$ and $S\setminus L$.** A point of $S\setminus L$ is not on the vertical line, so it is aligned with a point of $L$ only through a common $y$-coordinate. The points of $L$ have distinct $y$-coordinates, so each point of $S\setminus L$ is aligned with at most one point of $L$. For each point of $L$, the horizontal line through it contains at most $k$ points of $S$ (maximality of $k$), hence at most $k$ points of $S\setminus L$. So the number of points of $S\setminus L$ aligned with some point of $L$ is at most $k\cdot k=k^2$, and also at most $n$. Therefore it is at most $\min(k^2,n)\le\sqrt{k^2\cdot n}=k\sqrt n$, and so there are at most $k\sqrt n$ aligned pairs between $L$ and $S\setminus L$.

**Induction.** By hypothesis $S\setminus L$ (with $n-k<n$ points) can be partitioned into collinear sets with at most $(n-k)^{3/2}$ aligned pairs in different parts. Adding $L$ as one more part gives a partition of $S$ with at most
$$(n-k)^{3/2}+k\sqrt n\le(n-k)\sqrt n+k\sqrt n=n^{3/2}$$
aligned pairs in different parts. ∎
